figs.title: Elliptic and rectangular span loading
figs.caption: At equal lift and span, elliptic loading gives uniform downwash and the least induced drag, with e = 1. An untwisted rectangular wing carries more lift outboard, so its downwash grows toward the tips and its span efficiency is lower.

figs.title: Drag polar and the tangent for best L/D
figs.caption: The parabolic polar starts at C_D0 on the C_D axis. A line from the origin has slope C_L/C_D, so the steepest line that touches the polar marks (L/D)_max, where induced drag equals parasite drag.

figs.title: Jet thrust and drag versus speed
figs.caption: Total drag is the sum of parasite drag rising as V² and induced drag falling as 1/V², with its minimum at V_md. Jet thrust is close to constant with speed, so it crosses the drag curve twice, at V_min and V_max; the stall speed also bounds the low end.

figs.title: Brayton cycle on p-v axes
figs.caption: Air is compressed isentropically by ram and compressor from 0 to 3, heated at constant pressure from 3 to 4, and expanded through the turbine and nozzle from 4 to 9. The enclosed area is the net work that becomes jet kinetic energy.

figs.title: Helicopter power versus forward speed
figs.caption: Power required forms a bucket: induced power falls with speed, profile power rises gently, and parasite power grows as V³. The bottom of the bucket gives best endurance, and the tangent from the origin gives best range.

figs.title: Rotor sizing on Mars and Earth
figs.caption: Ideal hover power is T^(3/2)/√(2ρA). Mars gravity is about 0.38 of Earth's while its air is about 1/72 as dense, so for the same vehicle and power the rotor must be about twice the radius.

figs.title: Empty weight trend and the sizing loop
figs.caption: The historical trend for W_e/W₀ falls slowly with size, while the fraction left after fuel and payload rises with W₀. Iterating between the two curves converges on the takeoff weight where they cross.

figs.title: Divergence of a typical section
figs.caption: Lift acting at the aerodynamic centre ahead of the elastic axis twists the section nose up, which adds lift and more twist. Twist grows as (q/q_D)/(1 − q/q_D) and rises steeply as q approaches the divergence pressure q_D = k_θ/(SeC_Lα).

figs.title: Body, stability and wind axes
figs.caption: Body axes are fixed to the airframe, the wind axis points along the velocity, and the stability axis lies between them in the plane of symmetry. In wings level flight the pitch angle is θ = γ + α, and β measures sideslip out of the plane of symmetry.

figs.title: Level turn rate versus speed
figs.caption: Turn rate is bounded by C_Lmax at low speed and by the structural load limit at high speed, and these meet at the corner speed with the highest instantaneous turn rate. Sustained turns, where thrust equals drag, sit below this boundary.

figs.title: Drag buildup by source
figs.caption: Parasite drag is built from skin friction scaled by form factor and interference for each component, plus miscellaneous items. Induced drag and wave drag are added on top to give the cruise drag coefficient.

figs.title: Flap and slat types
figs.caption: Each device raises the airfoil maximum lift by a typical increment: plain and split flaps about 0.9, slotted flaps more, and Fowler and multi slotted flaps also extend the chord. The wing increment scales by the flapped area ratio and the cosine of the hinge line sweep.

figs.caption: Wing lift, the wing pitching moment and tail lift together set the moment about the CG. The neutral point is the CG position with zero pitch stiffness, and the static margin is how far the CG sits ahead of it, in mean chords.

figs.title: Gust load lines on the V-n diagram
figs.caption: Gust lines start at n = 1 and grow with equivalent airspeed at a slope set by the design gust velocity and the gust alleviation factor K_g. At light wing loading the gust envelope extends beyond the maneuver limits and sets the design load factor.
